questions.question: A client offers a relative the same insulin pen with a new needle. Which teaching is correct?

options.A: Only the needle is patient-specific
options.B: The whole pen must remain single-patient use
options.C: Matching insulin doses make sharing safe
options.D: Cleaning the outside makes sharing safe

rationales.A: The pen itself is patient-specific.
rationales.B: Needle replacement does not remove the pen-sharing infection risk.
rationales.C: Matching doses do not remove infection risk.
rationales.D: External cleaning does not establish safe sharing.

questions.category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

questions.question: Two clients need identical insulin. Which supplies must not be interchanged between them?

options.A: Their insulin pens, even with new needles
options.B: Unused single-use needles still in separate intact packages as allocated by policy
options.C: New unopened alcohol swabs allocated by policy
options.D: Unused sealed dressings allocated by policy

rationales.A: An in-use pen belongs to one patient; unused packaged supplies are different.
rationales.B: Unused intact supplies are not used patient-specific pens.
rationales.C: Unused sealed swabs do not involve pen sharing.
rationales.D: Unused sealed dressings do not involve pen sharing.

questions.category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

questions.question: An adult prescribed NITROSTAT sublingual tablets asks whether to transfer them into a weekly pill organizer. Which storage instruction is correct?

options.A: Keep them in their original glass container and close the cap tightly after each use.
options.B: Store the week's tablets loose in the organizer.
options.C: Keep several tablets in an unsealed pocket for quick access.
options.D: Remove the cap between uses to prevent moisture buildup.

rationales.A: The product label specifies the original glass container with a tightly closed cap to protect potency.
rationales.B: Transfer to the organizer does not follow the labeled storage instruction.
rationales.C: Loose, unsealed storage does not protect the product as directed.
rationales.D: Leaving the container open conflicts with the instruction.

questions.question: A client transfers NITROSTAT tablets from the original bottle to a plastic weekly box. What teaching is needed?

options.A: The organizer preserves potency equally by appearance alone
options.B: Leave the bottle open between uses
options.C: Keep them in the original tightly capped glass container
options.D: Store tablets loose in a wallet

rationales.A: Appearance does not establish equivalent storage.
rationales.B: The cap should be closed tightly.
rationales.C: The product has specific container requirements.
rationales.D: Loose wallet storage does not follow the label.

questions.question: After taking a NITROSTAT tablet, which storage action is appropriate?

options.A: Leave the cap off for ventilation
options.B: Tightly recap the original glass container
options.C: Transfer remaining tablets into a paper envelope
options.D: Mix them into another drug's bottle

rationales.A: Ventilation is not the storage instruction.
rationales.B: Recapping protects the product as labeled.
rationales.C: An envelope is not the original container.
rationales.D: Another medicine's bottle is not appropriate labeled storage.

questions.question: A clinician has diagnosed an uncomplicated viral cold with no bacterial infection. The client asks why an antibiotic was not prescribed. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: An antibiotic is needed once nasal mucus turns yellow.
options.B: Antibiotics shorten all colds if started early.
options.C: Antibiotics do not treat the virus causing this cold and can still cause adverse effects.
options.D: A smaller antibiotic dose treats viruses while a larger dose treats bacteria.

rationales.C: Antibiotics do not treat viral colds; unnecessary use adds risk without treating the cause.
rationales.A: Mucus color alone does not establish a need for antibiotics.
rationales.B: Early use does not make antibiotics effective against cold viruses.
rationales.D: Changing the dose does not turn an antibiotic into an antiviral.

questions.question: A clinician diagnoses a viral cold without bacterial infection. Yellow mucus appears. What teaching fits this diagnosis?

options.A: Color alone does not make antibiotics effective against the virus
options.B: Yellow mucus proves an antibiotic is required
options.C: An antibiotic treats all respiratory viruses
options.D: Using leftover antibiotics prevents all complications

rationales.A: Mucus color alone does not establish bacterial disease.
rationales.B: That conclusion is unsupported.
rationales.C: Antibiotics do not treat viruses.
rationales.D: Leftovers are not a justified prevention strategy.

questions.question: Why avoid an unneeded antibiotic for a confirmed uncomplicated viral cold?

options.A: All antibiotics are harmless if taken briefly
options.B: A low dose becomes an antiviral
options.C: Different brand names eliminate adverse effects
options.D: It does not treat the viral cause and still has adverse-effect risks

rationales.A: Brief use is not risk-free.
rationales.B: Dose reduction does not change its target into a virus.
rationales.C: Branding does not remove adverse effects.
rationales.D: Benefit and risk must match the actual indication.

questions.question: An adult newly prescribed an oral opioid analgesic asks about drinking alcohol during treatment. Which teaching is appropriate?

options.A: Avoid alcohol; combining it with the opioid can cause dangerous sedation and slowed breathing.
options.B: Alcohol is acceptable if it is taken with food.
options.C: Alcohol prevents opioid-related drowsiness.
options.D: A two-hour separation guarantees that the combination is safe.

rationales.A: Alcohol and opioids can compound central nervous system depression, including respiratory depression.
rationales.B: Food does not establish safety for this combination.
rationales.C: Alcohol does not counter the depressant effects.
rationales.D: A universal two-hour interval is not a safety guarantee.

questions.question: A client plans alcohol two hours after an opioid dose. Which response is appropriate?

options.A: Two hours guarantees safety
options.B: No universal two-hour gap makes that combination safe; avoid alcohol
options.C: Food eliminates breathing risk
options.D: Alcohol counteracts opioid sedation

rationales.A: That time rule is unsupported.
rationales.B: Alcohol can add to central nervous system depression.
rationales.C: Food does not establish safety.
rationales.D: Alcohol is not an antidote to sedation.

questions.question: Which discharge statement requires correction during opioid treatment?

options.A: I should avoid alcohol
options.B: Alcohol is safe if I take it with dinner
options.C: I should discuss other sedating medicines with my clinician
options.D: I should follow the medication guide

rationales.A: Avoidance is appropriate.
rationales.B: Eating does not eliminate the dangerous depressant combination.
rationales.C: Other depressants also require review.
rationales.D: Following product guidance is appropriate.

questions.question: A caregiver has an oral liquid medicine with a prescribed dose written in mL. Which device should the nurse recommend for measuring it?

options.A: A household teaspoon filled to the usual level.
options.B: A pharmacist-supplied oral dosing syringe with mL markings appropriate for the prescribed volume.
options.C: A kitchen tablespoon, estimating the needed fraction.
options.D: An unmarked cup used for other medicines.

rationales.B: A medication-measuring device with matching units and suitable graduations avoids household-spoon and estimation errors.
rationales.A: Household teaspoons are not a substitute for a dosing device.
rationales.C: Estimating a fraction of a kitchen spoon is unreliable.
rationales.D: An unmarked cup cannot measure the prescribed mL accurately.

questions.question: A caregiver has a liquid dose in mL but only an unmarked kitchen spoon. What should they obtain?

options.A: A larger kitchen spoon
options.B: An appropriate medication-measuring device marked in mL
options.C: An unmarked cup
options.D: A visual estimate from the bottle cap

rationales.A: A larger spoon does not provide calibration.
rationales.B: The device needs accurate matching graduations.
rationales.C: An unmarked cup cannot measure the prescribed volume.
rationales.D: Visual estimation is not reliable dosing.

questions.question: Which caregiver demonstration needs correction?

options.A: Using the pharmacist-provided oral syringe's mL scale
options.B: Estimating liquid medicine with a household teaspoon
options.C: Confirming the prescribed volume
options.D: Asking about unfamiliar device markings

rationales.A: The matched device is appropriate.
rationales.B: A kitchen spoon is not a calibrated medication device.
rationales.C: Dose verification is appropriate.
rationales.D: Clarification prevents measurement errors.

questions.question: During medication reconciliation, an adult lists prescription medicines but leaves out an occasional OTC sleep aid, vitamins, and an herbal supplement. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Record only prescriptions because OTC products do not interact with them.
options.B: Record supplements only if they are taken every day.
options.C: Wait until the client reports an adverse effect to add these products.
options.D: Include the OTC products and supplements, with their amounts and frequency, in the medication history.

rationales.D: A useful medication history includes prescription and nonprescription products and supplements, including intermittent use.
rationales.A: Nonprescription status does not rule out interactions.
rationales.B: Intermittent use still matters to the history.
rationales.C: Review should not depend on an adverse effect already occurring.

questions.question: A client uses an herbal product only on weekends. Should it appear in the medication history?

options.A: No, only daily products count
options.B: No, herbs cannot interact
options.C: Only after an adverse event
options.D: Yes, record the product and actual use

rationales.A: Frequency does not exclude them.
rationales.B: Natural origin does not rule out interactions.
rationales.C: History should be collected before harm occurs.
rationales.D: Intermittent supplements remain relevant to medication review.

questions.question: After a prescription dose changes, what should the client do with the medication list?

options.A: Keep the old dose until the next annual visit
options.B: Remove all OTC products
options.C: List only brand names without instructions
options.D: Update it and share the current version with the care team

rationales.A: An outdated dose can mislead care.
rationales.B: OTC use remains relevant.
rationales.C: Usage instructions are part of a useful list.
rationales.D: A current list supports accurate reconciliation.

questions.question: A client changes to a different manufacturer's tablet of the same medicine and strength. The previous tablet was approved for splitting. Before splitting the replacement, what should the nurse advise?

options.A: Assume both products can be split because the active ingredient is the same.
options.B: Decide from the tablet's color and size.
options.C: Confirm with the pharmacist or prescriber that the replacement product can be split as prescribed.
options.D: Split it whenever doing so lowers the cost, regardless of the label.

rationales.C: Manufacturers can formulate tablets differently. Permission to split one product does not automatically apply to another.
rationales.A: A shared ingredient does not establish equivalent splitting instructions.
rationales.B: Appearance does not establish suitability for splitting.
rationales.D: Cost does not override formulation and dosing considerations.

questions.question: A new manufacturer supplies a tablet previously split by the client. What determines whether to keep splitting?

options.A: The old tablet's instructions alone
options.B: A similar color
options.C: The price per tablet
options.D: The new product's verified splitting instructions

rationales.A: Permission does not automatically transfer.
rationales.B: Color does not establish suitability.
rationales.C: Cost does not establish formulation safety.
rationales.D: Formulations may differ across products.

questions.question: A client sees a score line and assumes any tablet can be divided safely. What is appropriate?

options.A: Use the line as the only criterion
options.B: Verify that the exact product and prescribed use permit splitting
options.C: Assume all capsules can also be divided
options.D: Crush instead if uncertain

rationales.A: Appearance alone is insufficient.
rationales.B: A product-specific check is needed.
rationales.C: Capsules have different formulation instructions.
rationales.D: Crushing is not a safe default.

questions.question: An adult feels better partway through a prescribed antibiotic course, reports no adverse effects, and has received no revised instructions. Which statement shows appropriate understanding?

options.A: I will save the remaining doses for a future illness.
options.B: I will give the remaining doses to a relative with similar symptoms.
options.C: I will reduce the frequency myself because the symptoms improved.
options.D: I will follow the prescribed course and contact my prescriber if I have concerns or need the plan reviewed.

rationales.D: Improvement alone does not authorize a patient to change the prescribed course.
rationales.A: Saving antibiotics for a later illness is not appropriate use.
rationales.B: Antibiotics should not be shared.
rationales.C: Frequency changes require clinical review.

questions.question: A prescriber changes an antibiotic plan after reviewing new results. Which instruction should the client follow?

options.A: The old plan regardless of new instructions
options.B: The revised prescribed plan
options.C: A relative's suggested schedule
options.D: A self-selected shorter schedule

rationales.A: Following prescriptions does not mean ignoring a revised order.
rationales.B: Current clinician instructions govern the course.
rationales.C: A relative cannot replace the treatment plan.
rationales.D: Independent schedule changes are inappropriate.

questions.question: A client feels better during an antibiotic course with no adverse effects and no revised order. What should happen?

options.A: Save remaining doses for another illness
options.B: Share remaining doses
options.C: Continue the prescribed plan and seek advice about concerns
options.D: Reduce frequency independently

rationales.A: Future illness needs its own assessment.
rationales.B: Prescriptions should not be shared.
rationales.C: Improvement alone does not authorize changing the regimen.
rationales.D: Dose scheduling changes need review.

questions.question: While reviewing medicines at home, an adult finds an expired OTC medicine for a nonurgent symptom. The tablets look unchanged. Which response is appropriate?

options.A: Do not use it; obtain an in-date product if needed and follow safe disposal guidance.
options.B: Use it because unchanged appearance proves full potency.
options.C: Take twice the labeled amount to compensate for possible loss of strength.
options.D: Refrigerate it overnight to restore its shelf life.

rationales.A: Appearance does not establish that an expired medicine remains safe and effective. FDA advises against using expired medicines.
rationales.B: Appearance is not a potency or safety test.
rationales.C: Increasing the dose is not a safe response to uncertainty.
rationales.D: Refrigeration does not reset the expiration date.

questions.question: An adult finds an expired OTC medicine for a nonurgent symptom. The package was stored as directed and the tablets look normal. Which action is appropriate?

options.A: Use it because storage instructions were followed
options.B: Try one dose and judge its strength by symptom relief
options.C: Use it if the package has never been opened
options.D: Replace it with an in-date product if needed and dispose of it safely

rationales.A: Correct storage does not extend the labeled expiration date.
rationales.B: A trial dose does not establish safety or potency.
rationales.C: An unopened package still has an expiration date.
rationales.D: Do not use an expired medicine; appearance cannot establish continued safety or effectiveness.

questions.question: A client finds an unopened OTC medicine past its printed expiration date. The symptom is nonurgent. Which response to the client is appropriate?

options.A: The intact seal extends the printed expiration date
options.B: A normal color is enough to confirm that it remains usable
options.C: Do not use it; obtain an in-date product if needed
options.D: A smaller dose makes an expired product suitable to try

rationales.A: The intact seal does not extend the labeled date.
rationales.B: Color cannot establish safety and effectiveness after expiry.
rationales.C: FDA advises not using expired medicines, including those that look unchanged.
rationales.D: Reducing a dose does not resolve uncertainty about an expired product.

questions.question: A client wants to check whether two OTC products contain the same medicine and how much each dose contains. Which Drug Facts section is the most direct place to look?

options.A: Uses.
options.B: Inactive ingredients.
options.C: Active ingredient(s).
options.D: Other information.

rationales.C: This section identifies therapeutic ingredients and their amounts per dosage unit.
rationales.A: Uses describes the conditions or symptoms treated.
rationales.B: Inactive ingredients are not the therapeutic ingredients being compared.
rationales.D: Other information includes matters such as storage, not the main active-ingredient listing.

questions.question: Where on an OTC Drug Facts label does a client find the amount of each therapeutic ingredient per dosage unit?

options.A: Inactive ingredients
options.B: Other information
options.C: Manufacturer address
options.D: Active ingredient(s)

rationales.A: Inactive ingredients are not the therapeutic dose.
rationales.B: Other information is not the main dose-ingredient listing.
rationales.C: An address does not identify the dose.
rationales.D: The active-ingredient section identifies medicine and amount.

questions.question: Two OTC products advertise different uses. What should be compared to detect duplication?

options.A: Their active ingredients
options.B: Only the Uses headings
options.C: Only the package size
options.D: Only the flavor

rationales.A: Different advertised uses can share an active medicine.
rationales.B: Uses alone may miss duplication.
rationales.C: Size does not identify the ingredient.
rationales.D: Flavor is not the therapeutic ingredient.

questions.question: An adult has unused tablets, no conflicting product-specific disposal instructions, and ready access to an authorized take-back location that accepts them. Which disposal plan should the nurse recommend?

options.A: Flush every tablet because all medicines belong on the flush list.
options.B: Use the authorized medication take-back location.
options.C: Leave the tablets loose in an open household wastebasket.
options.D: Give them to a neighbor who takes the same medicine.

rationales.B: An available authorized take-back option is the preferred disposal route for most unused medicines.
rationales.A: The FDA flush list is limited; flushing is not the default for all medicines.
rationales.C: Loose tablets in accessible waste can expose others.
rationales.D: Unused prescriptions should not be redistributed to another person.

questions.question: No nearby take-back site is available, but an authorized prepaid medicine mail-back option is ready. What is appropriate?

options.A: Give tablets to a neighbor
options.B: Flush every medicine indiscriminately
options.C: Use the approved mail-back option
options.D: Leave tablets loose in accessible trash

rationales.A: Medicines should not be redistributed informally.
rationales.B: Flushing is limited to specific guidance.
rationales.C: Approved mail-back is a take-back route.
rationales.D: Loose accessible medicines risk exposure.

questions.question: A medicine is on the FDA flush list and no take-back option is readily available. What instruction fits FDA guidance?

options.A: Assume medicines must never be flushed under any circumstances
options.B: Follow its specific flushing instructions
options.C: Give it to another person instead
options.D: Leave it indefinitely within children's reach

rationales.A: A universal ban misstates the exception.
rationales.B: FDA specifies a limited flushing exception when take-back is unavailable.
rationales.C: Sharing is not disposal.
rationales.D: Accessible storage can create exposure risk.

questions.question: After teaching a home-care plan, which question best checks understanding?

options.A: Do you understand?
options.B: Was my explanation clear?
options.C: How will you follow this plan at home?
options.D: Can you repeat my exact words?

rationales.A: A yes answer is insufficient.
rationales.B: This invites agreement rather than demonstration.
rationales.C: Teach-back checks understanding in the person's own words.
rationales.D: Recitation may conceal misunderstanding.

questions.question: A client's teach-back reveals confusion. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Blame poor memory
options.B: Explain differently and check again
options.C: Repeat faster
options.D: Document understanding anyway

rationales.A: Blame undermines communication.
rationales.B: Adapt the explanation and reassess understanding.
rationales.C: Speed does not resolve confusion.
rationales.D: Documentation should reflect the actual finding.

questions.question: A client reads discharge instructions aloud verbatim. What best checks their understanding?

options.A: Assume reading proves understanding
options.B: Ask only for a signature
options.C: Ask how they will apply the instructions
options.D: Stop further questions

rationales.A: Reading alone is insufficient.
rationales.B: A signature is not teach-back.
rationales.C: Application in their own words reveals understanding.
rationales.D: Questions may still be needed.

questions.question: An adult wants help quitting cigarettes. Which plan is evidence-supported?

options.A: Offer counseling and discuss suitable cessation medicines
options.B: Recommend willpower alone as the only effective method
options.C: Promise immediate success
options.D: Discourage asking for help

rationales.A: Counseling and medication can support quitting.
rationales.B: Support options exist.
rationales.C: Success cannot be guaranteed.
rationales.D: Help can improve the chance of quitting.

questions.question: A client wants confidential smoking-cessation coaching but cannot travel. Which resource fits?

options.A: An in-person-only requirement
options.B: A guaranteed-cure product
options.C: Advice to postpone indefinitely
options.D: Telephone quitline counseling

rationales.A: Travel is not required for all support.
rationales.B: Guaranteed cure claims are inappropriate.
rationales.C: A usable support option exists now.
rationales.D: Quitlines provide remote cessation support.

questions.question: A client says needing medication to quit means failure. What response fits?

options.A: Only unsupported quitting counts
options.B: Counseling and medicines cannot be combined
options.C: Medication guarantees permanent abstinence
options.D: Treatment can support a quit plan

rationales.A: That claim stigmatizes effective help.
rationales.B: They can be used together.
rationales.C: No guarantee is justified.
rationales.D: Treatment supports change without judging the client.

questions.question: An adult eligible for a routine injectable vaccine has a mild cold and no identified vaccine-specific contraindication. What is correct?

options.A: Every cold prohibits vaccination
options.B: Mild illness alone does not automatically require postponement
options.C: A negative viral test is always required
options.D: Only antibiotics permit vaccination

rationales.A: Mild illness is not a universal contraindication.
rationales.B: Screen for actual contraindications rather than assuming mild illness precludes vaccination.
rationales.C: That universal test requirement is unsupported.
rationales.D: Antibiotics are not a prerequisite.

questions.question: Vaccine screening identifies a moderate acute illness. What should happen?

options.A: Assess the precaution and generally defer until improved
options.B: Treat it identically to every mild cold
options.C: Ignore illness severity
options.D: Give every vaccine without screening

rationales.A: Moderate or severe illness is a precaution requiring assessment.
rationales.B: Severity matters.
rationales.C: Ignoring severity misses the precaution.
rationales.D: Screening remains necessary.

questions.question: Which statement needs correction during vaccine screening?

options.A: Screen before each dose
options.B: Any runny nose automatically prohibits vaccination
options.C: Check vaccine-specific contraindications
options.D: Assess illness severity

rationales.A: This is appropriate.
rationales.B: Mild symptoms alone are not a blanket prohibition.
rationales.C: This is necessary.
rationales.D: Severity influences the decision.

questions.question: Which position supports an accurate seated home BP measurement?

options.A: Legs crossed and arm dangling
options.B: Cuff over a thick sleeve
options.C: Talking throughout measurement
options.D: Back supported, feet flat, arm supported at heart level

rationales.A: This is not the recommended position.
rationales.B: Measure on the bare arm.
rationales.C: Talking can affect the reading.
rationales.D: Standardized positioning supports accurate measurement.

questions.question: A client rushes upstairs before a routine home BP check. What is appropriate?

options.A: Measure while still talking and moving
options.B: Rest quietly before measuring as instructed
options.C: Use a smaller cuff for convenience
options.D: Measure through clothing

rationales.A: Activity and talking impair standardization.
rationales.B: Quiet rest is part of standardized preparation.
rationales.C: Cuff size must fit.
rationales.D: The cuff belongs on bare skin.

questions.question: Home readings vary with different cuff sizes and positions. What should be reviewed?

options.A: Only the monitor's color
options.B: Only the room's decoration
options.C: Nothing if batteries work
options.D: Cuff fit and measurement technique

rationales.A: Color does not establish accuracy.
rationales.B: Decoration is irrelevant to technique.
rationales.C: Working batteries do not ensure correct measurement.
rationales.D: Technique and fit affect measurement accuracy.

questions.question: A client with established dementia needs extra time to respond. What communication approach helps?

options.A: Interrupt repeatedly
options.B: Speak about the client as absent
options.C: Argue over each memory error
options.D: Use simple choices and allow time

rationales.A: Interruption adds difficulty.
rationales.B: Exclusion is disrespectful.
rationales.C: Argument is not helpful communication.
rationales.D: Respectful clear communication supports participation.

questions.question: A client with dementia struggles with an open-ended beverage question. Which prompt may help?

options.A: Would you like some water?
options.B: Why can you never decide?
options.C: List every drink you remember
options.D: Answer faster, please

rationales.A: A simple choice reduces the communication burden.
rationales.B: Blame is unhelpful.
rationales.C: The memory demand adds difficulty.
rationales.D: Pressure reduces response time.

questions.question: During routine care, a client with dementia does not understand an instruction. What is appropriate?

options.A: Raise an angry voice
options.B: Ignore the client entirely
options.C: Try simpler wording and allow a response
options.D: Repeatedly test their memory

rationales.A: Anger is not clarification.
rationales.B: The client should remain included.
rationales.C: Adapt language while maintaining respect.
rationales.D: Memory testing is not the needed care instruction.

questions.question: A stable client expresses anxiety about tomorrow's procedure. Which response invites discussion?

options.A: Nothing can go wrong
options.B: What concerns you most about it?
options.C: You should not feel anxious
options.D: Other people have worse problems

rationales.A: This promises an uncertain outcome.
rationales.B: An open question explores the person's concerns.
rationales.C: This dismisses feelings.
rationales.D: Comparison minimizes the concern.

questions.question: A client worries about recovery after an elective procedure. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Guarantee painless recovery
options.B: Listen and clarify the specific concern
options.C: Immediately change the subject
options.D: Assume the concern is irrational

rationales.A: A guarantee is unjustified.
rationales.B: Listening guides useful information and support.
rationales.C: Avoidance blocks discussion.
rationales.D: Assumption replaces assessment.

questions.question: Which response to nonurgent procedural anxiety needs correction?

options.A: Tell me what worries you
options.B: I promise there are no risks
options.C: We can discuss your questions
options.D: Let us review the information together

rationales.A: This invites discussion.
rationales.B: False reassurance misrepresents uncertainty.
rationales.C: This supports participation.
rationales.D: This supports understanding.

questions.question: A recently bereaved adult wants to talk about their spouse. Which response is supportive?

options.A: Insist they stop mentioning the spouse
options.B: Set a fixed deadline for grief
options.C: Promise they will feel fine tomorrow
options.D: Invite them to share and listen

rationales.A: Avoidance may block wanted support.
rationales.B: Grief does not follow an imposed deadline.
rationales.C: The promise is unsupported.
rationales.D: Listening can support an individual grieving process.

questions.question: A bereaved adult asks about support beyond family. What can the nurse offer?

options.A: A rule against discussing loss
options.B: A guaranteed recovery date
options.C: A claim that needing help is failure
options.D: Information about bereavement counseling or groups

rationales.A: Discussion can be helpful.
rationales.B: Recovery cannot be scheduled this way.
rationales.C: Seeking support is not failure.
rationales.D: Counseling and peer support are available options.

questions.question: Two adults grieve differently after similar losses. Which approach is appropriate?

options.A: Require identical grieving behavior
options.B: Explore each person's needs and preferred support
options.C: Judge the quieter person as unaffected
options.D: Demand both follow the same timetable

rationales.A: Grief varies.
rationales.B: Support should be responsive to the individual.
rationales.C: Outward behavior does not establish absence of grief.
rationales.D: An imposed timetable is inappropriate.

questions.question: After immediate safety concerns are assessed, a client distressed by a known hallucination says they hear frightening voices. Which response is therapeutic?

options.A: I hear the same voices
options.B: You are lying
options.C: That sounds frightening; I want to understand how you feel
options.D: Argue until the client admits the voices are false

rationales.A: This reinforces the perception as shared reality.
rationales.B: Accusation damages trust.
rationales.C: Acknowledge distress without affirming the perception.
rationales.D: Confrontation is not supportive.

questions.question: A care plan addresses recurring hallucinations with no new safety concern. Which communication approach fits?

options.A: Confirm the belief is true
options.B: Listen calmly without agreeing with the belief
options.C: Ridicule the experience
options.D: Debate aggressively

rationales.A: Agreement validates the belief as fact.
rationales.B: Support feelings while avoiding reinforcement.
rationales.C: Ridicule undermines trust.
rationales.D: Argument may worsen distress.

questions.question: A client asks whether the nurse shares their unusual perception. Which response fits, after safety assessment?

options.A: Yes, it is definitely real
options.B: I do not experience that, but I can see it upsets you
options.C: Stop talking nonsense
options.D: Everyone is secretly watching you

rationales.A: False agreement reinforces the perception.
rationales.B: Honesty and emotional acknowledgment can coexist.
rationales.C: Dismissal is unhelpful.
rationales.D: This adds to the distressing belief.

questions.question: An adult at pressure-injury risk has vulnerable sacral skin. Which proposed preventive action should be avoided?

options.A: Use the assessed repositioning plan
options.B: Inspect the skin
options.C: Provide appropriate pressure redistribution
options.D: Firmly massage the area

rationales.A: Repositioning is part of prevention.
rationales.B: Inspection supports assessment.
rationales.C: Pressure redistribution can help.
rationales.D: Massage or rubbing is not recommended prevention.

questions.question: A caregiver proposes rubbing reddened skin to prevent a pressure injury. What is appropriate?

options.A: Rub harder to restore color
options.B: Avoid rubbing and arrange assessment with pressure relief
options.C: Wait for open skin before acting
options.D: Ignore the finding if painless

rationales.A: Rubbing is not recommended.
rationales.B: Avoid damaging friction and assess the skin promptly.
rationales.C: Prevention precedes breakdown.
rationales.D: Painlessness does not rule out risk.

questions.question: Which pressure-injury prevention instruction needs correction?

options.A: Follow an individualized repositioning plan
options.B: Assess skin regularly
options.C: Massage bony areas vigorously
options.D: Use suitable support surfaces

rationales.A: The plan should reflect assessed needs.
rationales.B: Assessment supports prevention.
rationales.C: Massage is not recommended preventive care.
rationales.D: Appropriate surfaces support pressure redistribution.

questions.question: Where should an indwelling urinary catheter's drainage bag be positioned?

options.A: Above the bladder
options.B: On the floor
options.C: Below bladder level and off the floor
options.D: With the tube tightly kinked

rationales.A: This risks backflow.
rationales.B: Floor contact is inappropriate.
rationales.C: Dependent unobstructed drainage is recommended.
rationales.D: Kinking obstructs flow.

questions.question: During transfer, the drainage bag is placed on the client's abdomen. What should be corrected?

options.A: Leave it above the bladder
options.B: Disconnect routinely for convenience
options.C: Place it on the floor
options.D: Secure it below bladder level without kinking tubing

rationales.A: The bag should remain below the bladder.
rationales.B: Unnecessary disconnection breaks the system.
rationales.C: The floor is not an appropriate location.
rationales.D: Maintain dependent flow and the closed system.

questions.question: A catheter tube is kinked beneath a bedrail. Which action addresses this maintenance problem?

options.A: Tighten the kink
options.B: Raise the bag above the bladder
options.C: Disconnect without indication
options.D: Restore unobstructed tubing and assess drainage

rationales.A: This worsens obstruction.
rationales.B: Raising the bag is inappropriate.
rationales.C: Unnecessary disconnection risks contamination.
rationales.D: Unobstructed flow is a maintenance requirement.

questions.question: An adult with dry mouth can swallow safely and has no fluid restriction. Which comfort measure is appropriate?

options.A: Frequent small sips of water
options.B: Routine alcohol-containing drinks
options.C: Avoiding all fluids
options.D: Stopping prescribed medicines independently

rationales.A: Water can relieve dryness within the care plan.
rationales.B: Alcohol can worsen dryness.
rationales.C: Fluid avoidance does not relieve it.
rationales.D: Medication changes require review.

questions.question: A client with dry mouth and a prescribed fluid limit asks for advice. What is appropriate?

options.A: Ignore the fluid limit
options.B: Adapt oral comfort measures with the care team within the limit
options.C: Stop all oral care
options.D: Double all drinks automatically

rationales.A: The prescribed limit still matters.
rationales.B: Comfort advice must fit the person's restrictions.
rationales.C: Oral care remains important.
rationales.D: Automatic increases disregard the plan.

questions.question: An adult with safe swallowing asks about sugarless gum for dry mouth. What is correct?

options.A: It may stimulate saliva when suitable for the person
options.B: Only sugary candy can help
options.C: Dry mouth means oral hygiene is unnecessary
options.D: Any medicine causing dryness must be stopped immediately

rationales.A: Sugarless gum is a suggested comfort measure.
rationales.B: Sugar is not required for this purpose.
rationales.C: Oral hygiene remains important.
rationales.D: Suspected adverse effects require review, not unilateral cessation.

questions.question: Which home environment supports sleep habits?

options.A: A quiet, dark, comfortably cool room
options.B: Bright screens throughout the night
options.C: Loud television all night
options.D: A different sleep schedule every day

rationales.A: A sleep-friendly environment supports rest.
rationales.B: Screen light can disrupt sleep.
rationales.C: Noise may interfere with sleep.
rationales.D: Irregular timing can disrupt routines.

questions.question: An adult has difficulty settling after late-night screen use. Which habit is reasonable to discuss?

options.A: Increase screen brightness
options.B: Keep television on continuously
options.C: Reduce screen exposure before sleep
options.D: Assume environment cannot affect sleep

rationales.A: More light does not address the issue.
rationales.B: Continuous stimulation may worsen it.
rationales.C: Light and stimulation can interfere with sleep routines.
rationales.D: Environment can matter.

questions.question: Which plan supports a consistent home sleep routine?

options.A: Alternate sleep times widely each day
options.B: Use bright lights all night
options.C: Keep similar bedtime and waking times
options.D: Replace sleep with television

rationales.A: Large shifts undermine consistency.
rationales.B: Bright light is not sleep-friendly.
rationales.C: Regular timing supports sleep habits.
rationales.D: Television does not replace sleep.

questions.question: A peripheral IV carrying nonvesicant saline becomes warm, red, and tender along the vein. What is appropriate?

options.A: Continue because fluid still runs
options.B: Stop using it, assess, and remove the affected catheter per protocol
options.C: Increase the infusion rate
options.D: Cover the redness and ignore it

rationales.A: Flow does not rule out complications.
rationales.B: These findings suggest phlebitis; the catheter should not remain in use.
rationales.C: Increasing flow does not address inflammation.
rationales.D: Concealment delays care.

questions.question: Which peripheral-IV finding requires action even if the infusion still flows?

options.A: An intact clean dressing
options.B: New tenderness and redness along the vein
options.C: A dry connection
options.D: Comfort without swelling or redness

rationales.A: An intact dressing is not the complication described.
rationales.B: Flow does not exclude phlebitis.
rationales.C: A dry connection alone is not a warning sign.
rationales.D: No complication is described.

questions.question: A nonvesicant peripheral IV shows phlebitis. Why is routine continued use inappropriate?

options.A: Only a blocked line can be problematic
options.B: Local inflammatory signs warrant assessment and removal
options.C: Redness always proves no risk
options.D: Infusion rate determines whether redness matters

rationales.A: Complications can occur with flow.
rationales.B: Phlebitis is an indication to remove the catheter.
rationales.C: Redness is not reassurance.
rationales.D: Rate alone does not resolve the finding.

questions.question: An adult develops new black tarry stool and lightheadedness. Which response is appropriate?

options.A: Wait a week
options.B: Assume color proves a harmless food effect
options.C: Arrange immediate assessment for possible GI bleeding
options.D: Recommend an extra OTC pain medicine

rationales.A: Delay can be unsafe.
rationales.B: The cause should not be assumed.
rationales.C: The combination can indicate significant bleeding.
rationales.D: Medication advice does not address the urgent assessment need.

questions.question: An adult vomits material resembling coffee grounds. What does this warrant?

options.A: Prompt medical evaluation
options.B: Routine observation until next month
options.C: A guaranteed diagnosis from appearance alone
options.D: Assurance that bleeding is impossible

rationales.A: This can be a GI bleeding sign.
rationales.B: Delay is inappropriate.
rationales.C: Evaluation is needed to establish cause.
rationales.D: The appearance can suggest bleeding.

questions.question: Why does black tarry stool with dizziness require assessment rather than automatic reassurance?

options.A: Every dark stool is proven hemorrhage
options.B: Dizziness excludes bleeding
options.C: Possible bleeding with systemic symptoms
options.D: Only painful bleeding matters

rationales.A: The symptom is not a definitive diagnosis alone.
rationales.B: Dizziness can accompany bleeding.
rationales.C: The pattern warrants evaluation without claiming certainty.
rationales.D: Bleeding can be serious without pain.

questions.question: At home after surgery, an adult develops sudden breathlessness and chest pain with breathing. What should be advised?

options.A: Call emergency services now
options.B: Wait for the next appointment
options.C: Assume normal recovery
options.D: Drive alone to a routine pharmacy

rationales.A: These can be pulmonary embolism symptoms requiring immediate care.
rationales.B: Delay is unsafe.
rationales.C: The new pattern should not be dismissed.
rationales.D: Emergency evaluation is needed.

questions.question: A postoperative client has sudden dyspnea but no leg swelling. What is correct?

options.A: Absence of leg symptoms does not exclude pulmonary embolism; escalate urgently
options.B: No swelling rules out PE
options.C: Only bilateral swelling matters
options.D: Observe without assessment

rationales.A: PE can occur without recognized DVT symptoms.
rationales.B: This rule is false.
rationales.C: Leg findings do not control emergency recognition.
rationales.D: New dyspnea requires prompt assessment.

questions.question: Which postoperative finding needs immediate assessment and escalation?

options.A: Unchanged mild incision soreness
options.B: A routine dressing question
options.C: A request for lunch
options.D: Sudden chest pain with unexplained breathlessness

rationales.A: No deterioration is described.
rationales.B: Routine questions are less urgent.
rationales.C: A meal request is less urgent.
rationales.D: The new respiratory pattern may represent a serious complication.

questions.question: Before a routine antibiotic dose, the client reports a past reaction absent from the record. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Ignore it because the chart is blank
options.B: Give it and ask later
options.C: Clarify and document the reaction and verify the plan before administration
options.D: Automatically label every medicine an allergy

rationales.A: The client's report matters.
rationales.B: Verification should precede exposure.
rationales.C: Reconcile the new allergy information before routine administration.
rationales.D: The history must be specific.

questions.question: Which allergy documentation is most useful?

options.A: Only the word allergy
options.B: Only the tablet color
options.C: Drug name, reaction symptoms, severity, and timing
options.D: Only the pharmacy location

rationales.A: A vague label omits needed information.
rationales.B: Color does not establish the reaction.
rationales.C: Specific details support safe decisions.
rationales.D: Location does not describe the allergy.

questions.question: A chart says no known allergies, but the client describes prior hives after a drug. What is appropriate?

options.A: Assume the electronic record is always correct
options.B: Delete the report without discussion
options.C: Reconcile the discrepancy and confirm drug-specific instructions
options.D: Test the drug casually at bedside

rationales.A: Records can be incomplete.
rationales.B: The report needs assessment.
rationales.C: Current patient information must inform verification.
rationales.D: An informal challenge is inappropriate.

questions.question: At home, an adult suddenly develops facial droop and slurred speech. What should a witness do?

options.A: Wait to see if it resolves
options.B: Offer a meal first
options.C: Drive alone later
options.D: Call emergency services immediately and note when symptoms began

rationales.A: Waiting delays care.
rationales.B: Feeding delays assessment and may be unsafe.
rationales.C: Emergency transport is preferred.
rationales.D: Possible stroke symptoms require time-sensitive emergency assessment.

questions.question: Sudden one-sided weakness improves before help arrives. What is appropriate?

options.A: Continue emergency evaluation
options.B: Cancel because improvement proves safety
options.C: Wait a week
options.D: Ignore the original symptoms

rationales.A: Transient improvement does not make the event safe to dismiss.
rationales.B: Improvement does not exclude a serious event.
rationales.C: Delay is inappropriate.
rationales.D: The episode still matters.

questions.question: Which information should accompany an emergency call for new stroke-like symptoms?

options.A: When the person was last known well and when changes were noticed
options.B: Only their preferred meal
options.C: Only next month's appointments
options.D: A guess that symptoms are harmless

rationales.A: Timing helps the emergency team assess treatment options.
rationales.B: This does not address the urgent event.
rationales.C: This is not the key timing information.
rationales.D: Reassurance without evaluation is unsafe.

questions.question: An alert adult with glucose 64 mg/dL can swallow safely. The ordered protocol uses the 15-15 rule. What is appropriate?

options.A: Give 15 g fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck after 15 minutes
options.B: Give diet soda
options.C: Wait until tomorrow
options.D: Give extra insulin

rationales.A: This follows the specified adult hypoglycemia protocol.
rationales.B: Diet soda lacks the needed sugar.
rationales.C: Treatment should not be delayed.
rationales.D: Extra insulin can worsen the low glucose.

questions.question: After protocol treatment, an alert adult's glucose remains 66 mg/dL at 15 minutes. What follows the ordered 15-15 plan?

options.A: Repeat fast-acting carbohydrate and reassess as directed
options.B: Stop checking because symptoms improved
options.C: Give extra insulin
options.D: Wait several hours

rationales.A: Persistent low glucose requires further protocol treatment and reassessment.
rationales.B: Symptoms alone do not confirm recovery.
rationales.C: Insulin could worsen hypoglycemia.
rationales.D: Prolonged delay is inappropriate.

questions.question: Which adult hypoglycemia situation fits oral fast-acting carbohydrate under protocol?

options.A: Unconscious and unable to swallow
options.B: Actively choking
options.C: Unable to protect the airway
options.D: Alert, safely swallowing, glucose 63 mg/dL

rationales.A: Do not give oral intake to an unconscious person.
rationales.B: Choking makes oral intake unsafe.
rationales.C: An unprotected airway makes oral intake unsafe.
rationales.D: Oral treatment requires safe swallowing and appropriate assessment.

questions.question: An adult at home has severe asthma-related breathing difficulty despite prescribed reliever treatment. What is appropriate?

options.A: Wait until the next routine visit
options.B: Call emergency services and follow the emergency action plan
options.C: Assume treatment failure is harmless
options.D: Go to sleep and reassess tomorrow

rationales.A: Routine delay is unsafe.
rationales.B: Severe unrelieved breathing difficulty requires emergency help.
rationales.C: Persistent severe symptoms are concerning.
rationales.D: Sleeping delays urgent assessment.

questions.question: Which asthma report warrants emergency escalation?

options.A: Symptoms resolved according to the action plan
options.B: Breathing remains very hard after reliever use
options.C: A routine refill question without symptoms
options.D: An upcoming follow-up question

rationales.A: The described symptoms have resolved.
rationales.B: Severe symptoms not relieved by treatment require help.
rationales.C: No acute deterioration is described.
rationales.D: This is routine planning.

questions.question: A client's asthma medicines have not relieved a severe attack. What should teaching emphasize?

options.A: Repeatedly exceeding prescribed doses without advice
options.B: Ignoring the action plan
options.C: Urgent emergency help rather than prolonged waiting
options.D: Waiting until morning regardless of severity

rationales.A: Unsupervised escalation is not the instruction.
rationales.B: The plan guides response.
rationales.C: Follow the emergency plan and obtain help for unrelieved severe symptoms.
rationales.D: Severity makes delay unsafe.

questions.question: Which daily-weight routine supports heart-failure monitoring?

options.A: Different scales at random times
options.B: Same scale, morning after urinating and before breakfast, similar clothing
options.C: Only after large meals
options.D: Only when shoes feel tight

rationales.A: Changing conditions adds variability.
rationales.B: Consistent conditions improve comparison across days.
rationales.C: Meals affect comparability.
rationales.D: Daily monitoring should not depend solely on symptoms.

questions.question: A client tracking heart-failure weights usually weighs before breakfast after urinating. Today the client weighs after breakfast in a heavy robe. What should the nurse emphasize for future measurements?

options.A: Average readings taken under different conditions without recording the differences
options.B: Change to evening measurements whenever the morning weight is higher
options.C: Use the same morning routine, scale, location, and similar clothing each day
options.D: Subtract an estimated amount for breakfast and clothing from each reading

rationales.A: Inconsistent conditions make the trend harder to interpret.
rationales.B: Switching times in response to a reading makes comparisons less consistent.
rationales.C: Consistent conditions improve comparison of daily measurements. Follow the care team’s reporting plan for concerning changes or symptoms.
rationales.D: Estimated adjustments are not a substitute for consistent measurement conditions.

questions.question: A client compares a morning weight without shoes with an evening weight in heavy clothing. What needs review?

options.A: Use consistent conditions before interpreting the trend
options.B: Assume the difference proves fluid overload
options.C: Stop all monitoring
options.D: Change medication solely from that comparison

rationales.A: Measurement conditions can contribute to the difference.
rationales.B: The comparison alone does not prove the cause.
rationales.C: Monitoring remains useful.
rationales.D: A poorly comparable reading should not drive unilateral dosing.
